info.bio:
Suzanne Vega, cantante y compositora, nació el 11 de julio de 1959 en Santa Mónica, Los Ángeles, California.

A los dos años de edad, se trasladó con su familia a Nueva York. Se crió en el barrio hispano de Harlem; a los nueve años escribió su primer poema y con catorce empezó a componer canciones. Cursó estudios de danza contemporánea y frecuentó los clubes de Greenwich Village mientras asistía a clases de literatura en la escuela de arte Barnard College.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.title: John Hughes Film Exposure (1980s)
podcast.body: Suzanne Vega's music was featured on the carefully curated soundtracks of John Hughes' 1980s films. These soundtracks played a significant role in introducing a wide audience in North America to various alternative rock artists, particularly British performers. "So many people learned of bands like The Specials and Spandovalet and Billy Idle and General Public and Wang Chung and Yellow and New Order and the Psychedelic Furs and the Smiths and Echo and the Bunyman, Susanne Vagan in excess the Jesus and Mary chain, Flesh for Luluo and so many others from those soundtrack albums."

podcast.title: Mother of the MP3
podcast.body: Suzanne Vega earned the title "the mother of the MP3" due to the instrumental role her song "Tom's Diner" played in the development and refinement of the MP3 compression algorithm. Its unique acapella nature made it an ideal audio file for researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute to test and perfect the technology. "That song and its use in the development of compression algorithm technology, the one we call MP3, is why we call Suzanne Vega the mother of the MP3."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music Questions People Almost Never Ask

podcast.title: Mother of the MP3
podcast.body: Although Suzanne Vega had no direct involvement with the technical aspects of the MP3, her 1987 a cappella recording was critically important in the development and refinement of the MP3 compression algorithms by the Fraunhofer Society. This made her historically recognized as the "mother of the MP3." "So although she had nothing to do with the tactical aspects of the MP3, Suzanne Vega has gone down in history as the mother of the MP3."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: Tom's Diner Location (New York City)
podcast.body: The diner that Suzanne Vega sings about in her song "Tom's Diner" was a real establishment located at 2800 Broadway in New York City. This specific diner later gained additional recognition by serving as the exterior shot for Monks Cafe in the popular television show "Seinfeld." "A little aside here, the Tom's diner about which Suzanne Vega sings existed at 2800 Broadway in New York City. It sat in for Monks Cafe on Seinfeld."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of the MP3

podcast.title: Tom's Restaurant Inspiration
podcast.body: The song "Tom's Diner" was written by Suzanne Vega while sitting in a booth at Tom's Restaurant, a real-life establishment located at the corner of Broadway and 112th Street in New York City. This same restaurant later gained additional fame as the exterior of Monk's Diner in the popular television series "Seinfeld." "By the way, that song was written in a booth at Tom's Restaurant, a real restaurant, on the corner of Broadway and 112th of New York. That's the same restaurant that served as Monks Diner in Seinfeld."
